devotional.title: Exodus 7: When God Hardens Hearts
overview: God's willingness to confront Pharaoh reveals a profound truth: the Lord works through persistent resistance, never backing down from His redemptive purposes, no matter how stubborn human hearts become.

When Moses hesitantly objected that Pharaoh would not listen, God made an extraordinary announcement. He would harden Pharaoh's heart so that the Egyptians might know that He is the Lord. This seems counterintuitive—why would God make things harder? Yet embedded here is a revelation about God's character: His power is not lessened by human refusal; rather, His glory is magnified through it. Sometimes the greatest display of God's might comes not through unopposed victory but through triumph over determined opposition. The plagues were not simply punishments; they were object lessons for all Egypt, demonstrations of God's supremacy over their gods.

Notice too that Aaron's staff becoming a snake—seemingly an impressive miracle—was easily replicated by Pharaoh's own magicians. God was teaching a patient lesson. The plagues would escalate in ways that Pharaoh's magic could not match. This mirrors the spiritual life we know: sometimes we test God with half-measures, thinking we can handle faith on our own terms, until circumstances strip away our illusions and leave us confronted with His undeniable reality.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart is also a mirror we must hold to ourselves. When God calls us toward change, toward obedience, toward costly discipleship, our resistance itself becomes a test. Each time we refuse to listen, our hearts grow harder. We become less capable of hearing His voice. This is not arbitrary punishment but the natural consequence of persistent refusal—we become what we repeatedly choose to be.

God's commitment to Israel's freedom was unshakeable, and it reveals His commitment to our freedom today. He does not tire of calling us. He works through our resistance, even our rebellion, because His purposes stand.
What resistance to God's calling have you noticed hardening in your own heart, and what might it take to soften it again?

scholarly.title: Exodus 7: Scholarly study
overview: Exodus 7 marks a pivotal transition in the narrative arc of Israel's deliverance, moving from preparatory commission to direct confrontation with Pharaoh. The chapter functions as both theological prologue and narrative catalyst for the plague sequence that will dominate chapters 7–12. Composed within the broader Priestly redaction while incorporating older Yahwistic traditions, this text establishes the theological framework through which ancient Israel understood divine power operating within and against imperial structures.

The chapter opens with Yahweh's remarkable declaration that Moses shall be "as God" (*ʾělōhîm*) to Pharaoh, with Aaron serving as his "prophet" (*nāḇîʾ*). This hierarchical arrangement mirrors the divine-prophetic relationship, establishing Moses's absolute authority in the Egyptian court while accommodating his earlier protests regarding speech. The term *ʾělōhîm* here functions not as ontological equation but as relational designation—Moses embodies divine authority before Egypt's ruler, inverting the Egyptian ideology wherein Pharaoh himself claimed divine status.

Central to the chapter's theology is the repeated declaration that Yahweh will "harden" (*qāšâ*, *ḥāzaq*) Pharaoh's heart. This hardening motif has generated extensive scholarly debate regarding divine sovereignty and human agency. The Hebrew employs multiple verbs—*ḥāzaq* (to strengthen), *kāḇēd* (to make heavy), and *qāšâ* (to make obstinate)—suggesting a complex interplay rather than simple determinism. Notably, the early plague narratives alternate between Pharaoh hardening his own heart and Yahweh effecting the hardening, indicating that divine action operates upon an already resistant will.

The staff-to-serpent sign performed before Pharaoh introduces the contest motif that structures the plagues. When Egyptian magicians replicate the sign through their "secret arts" (*lāṭîm*), the narrative acknowledges Egyptian magical competence while asserting Yahweh's superiority—Aaron's serpent swallows theirs. The Hebrew *tannîn* (serpent/dragon) carries mythological resonance, evoking chaos imagery that Egyptian royal ideology claimed Pharaoh controlled.

The first plague transforms the Nile—Egypt's source of life and object of veneration—into blood (*dām*), rendering it death-dealing. This assault strikes at Egypt's theological and economic foundation, demonstrating that Yahweh's sovereignty extends over nature itself, establishing the pattern of escalating confrontation that follows.

prophetic.title: Exodus 7: Prophetic perspective
overview: This chapter unfolds approximately 1446 years before the incarnation of Christ, at the threshold of Israel's deliverance from Egyptian bondage—a moment that would become the defining act of divine redemption in the Old Testament. Standing at the hinge point between the patriarchal promises to Abraham and their national fulfillment, Exodus 7 initiates the great contest between Yahweh and the gods of Egypt, between the kingdom of darkness and the coming kingdom of God.

Here Moses stands before Pharaoh not as a mere negotiator but as one made "as God to Pharaoh," with Aaron serving as his prophet. This divine commissioning establishes a pattern that reaches its fullness in Christ, the ultimate Prophet who speaks not merely for God but as God in human flesh. Where Moses was appointed to this role, Christ possesses it eternally; where Moses required Aaron as intermediary, Christ needs no mediator, being Himself the perfect Word made flesh.

The hardening of Pharaoh's heart reveals a sobering principle that echoes through Scripture to the final judgment: God's patience eventually gives way to His purposes, and resistance to divine mercy calcifies into judicial hardening. This pattern resurfaces in Romans 9, where Paul draws directly upon this narrative to illustrate God's sovereign freedom in salvation and judgment. Pharaoh becomes a type of all who harden themselves against the light—ultimately fulfilled in the beast and his followers who, despite seeing God's mighty works, curse rather than repent.

The transformation of Aaron's staff into a serpent, swallowing the magicians' serpents, prophetically demonstrates that though Satan counterfeits God's works, he is ultimately devoured by divine power. This anticipates the cross, where Christ, lifted up on a pole like the bronze serpent, destroys the serpent's work entirely. The first plague—water turned to blood—strikes at Hapi, Egypt's god of the Nile, declaring Yahweh's supremacy over all false deities. Yet this blood also points forward: blood that brings death to Egypt will soon bring life through the Passover lamb, and ultimately through the blood of the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin.

For the church awaiting Christ's return, this chapter proclaims that no earthly power, no spiritual counterfeit, and no hardened resistance can thwart God's redemptive purposes. The God who delivered Israel from Pharaoh will deliver His people from every oppressor, culminating in the final exodus from this age of sin into the eternal promised land.
